turns.prompt_text: I now own a Nintendo switch. I also have a PS4 controller. Is it possible to play my Nintendo switch with a PS4 controller? I'm sure it's possible with hacking, but is it possible without hacking?
turns.response_html:
Yes, it is absolutely possible to use a PS4 controller (DualShock 4) with a Nintendo Switch without any hacking or software modification. Since the Switch does not natively support third-party Bluetooth controllers from other consoles, you will need a small piece of hardware called a wireless USB adapter.

How It Works

These adapters act as a bridge. You plug the adapter into the Switch's USB port, and the adapter handles the Bluetooth connection with the PS4 controller. To the Switch, the adapter looks like a standard wired Pro Controller.

Recommended Adapters

The two most reliable options on the market are:

  • 8BitDo Wireless USB Adapter 2: Highly popular, compact, and supports button remapping and macros via their software.
  • Mayflash Magic-NS: Very versatile and often includes a USB-C to USB-A cable for handheld mode.

Step-by-Step Setup

  1. Enable Wired Communication: On your Switch, go to System Settings > Controllers and Sensors > Pro Controller Wired Communication and set it to On. This is the most important step; the adapter will not work without it.
  2. Plug in the Adapter:
    • Docked Mode: Plug the adapter into one of the USB ports on the side or inside the back of the dock.
    • Handheld/Switch Lite Mode: You will need a USB-C to USB-A (OTG) adapter to plug the dongle directly into the bottom of the Switch.
  3. Pairing:
    • Press the pairing button on the USB adapter (it will usually start flashing rapidly).
    • On your PS4 controller, hold the PS Button and the Share Button simultaneously until the light bar starts pulsing white.
    • Once the light bar turns a solid color, the controller is paired.

Important Considerations

  • Button Mapping: The Switch uses a different layout than PlayStation ($A/B$ and $X/Y$ are swapped). Most adapters automatically map the PS4's Circle to Switch A and Cross to Switch B, but you can usually customize this.
  • Features: You will keep vibration and motion controls (gyro) with most high-quality adapters. However, you cannot "wake" the Switch from sleep mode using the PS4 controller; you’ll need to press the power button on the console first.
  • One Adapter per Controller: If you want to connect two PS4 controllers, you will need two separate USB adapters.

turns.prompt_text: Can I use a Raspberry Pi Pico to do this?
turns.response_html:
Since you are interested in DIY hardware, using a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040) is an excellent way to do this. It allows you to build your own adapter that functions exactly like the commercial versions without any software modifications to your Nintendo Switch.

The project that makes this possible is PicoGamepadConverter.

Why it works

The RP2040 is unique because of its PIO (Programmable I/O). While the Pico only has one native hardware USB port, the PIO can "bit-bang" a second USB port into existence on the GPIO pins. This allows the Pico to act as a USB Host (reading your PS4 controller) and a USB Device (emulating a Switch Pro Controller) simultaneously.

Option A: The Wireless "Dongle" (Recommended)

If you have a Raspberry Pi Pico W, you can receive the PS4 controller's input via Bluetooth and send it to the Switch via the native USB port. This is the cleanest setup.

  1. Hardware: Raspberry Pi Pico W.
  2. Firmware: Flash the PicoGamepadConverter .uf2 file.
  3. Setup:
    • Put the Pico W into Configuration Mode (usually by holding the BOOTSEL button or a mapped GPIO button during power-on).
    • Connect it to your computer. It will appear as a network device or provide a web interface (typically at [http://192.168.3.1](http://192.168.3.1)).
    • Set the Host Mode to Bluetooth (PS4) and the Device Mode to Nintendo Switch.
    • Enter the Bluetooth MAC address of your PS4 controller into the web interface.

Option B: The Wired "Bridge"

If you have a standard Pico, you will need to add a second physical USB port to take the wired input from the PS4 controller.

  1. Hardware: Raspberry Pi Pico + a Female USB-A Breakout.
  2. Wiring: You will need to solder the USB breakout to specific GPIO pins (usually GP16 and GP17) to use the PIO USB Host capability.
    • VCC: Connect to the Pico's VBUS (5V).
    • D+ / D-: Connect to the designated PIO pins.
    • GND: Common ground.
  3. Firmware: Flash the same firmware but set the Host Mode to USB (Dinput/PS4).

Critical Switch Settings

Regardless of which hardware path you choose, you must change one setting on your console for the Switch to recognize the Pico as a controller:

  • Go to System Settings > Controllers and Sensors.
  • Set Pro Controller Wired Communication to On.

Pro-Tips for DIY Hardware

  • Latency: The RP2040 is incredibly fast. Most implementations of this project offer sub-$1ms$ input latency, which is often better than native Bluetooth connections.
  • Case Design: Since you have experience with 3D printing, this is a perfect candidate for a small custom enclosure or "dongle" style shell using your 90 alpha TPU for a rugged, grippy finish.
  • Power: The Pico will draw power directly from the Switch dock or the console’s USB-C port (if using an OTG adapter), so no external battery is required.

Would you like the specific GPIO pin mappings for the PIO USB host, or would you prefer to start with the Bluetooth configuration on a Pico W?
